claims.text: Conventionally cast MnNiSi-based magnetic-refrigeration alloys have a coarse-grained, defect-rich microstructure.
The conventionally cast baseline has a large magnetocaloric effect.
The conventionally cast baseline has suboptimal mechanical properties.
Melt spinning at a cooling rate above 10^5 K/s will produce a fine-grained MnNiSi-based microstructure.
Annealing at approximately 600°C for about 1 hour in an inert atmosphere will relieve residual stresses.
The specified short anneal will not promote significant grain growth.
Rapid solidification followed by short-time annealing will produce grain refinement and a more uniform microstructure.
The refined microstructure will provide enhanced grain-boundary strengthening.
Ultrafine grains will limit crack propagation.
Ultrafine grains will improve ductility through the Hall-Petch effect.
Brief annealing will mitigate residual stresses without causing significant grain coarsening.
Brief annealing will avoid phase transitions that would detract from magnetocaloric properties.
Preservation of the active magnetic phase will maintain the alloy's intrinsic magnetocaloric performance.
Rapid solidification followed by short annealing will increase ductility relative to the conventionally cast baseline.
Rapid solidification followed by short annealing will increase toughness relative to the conventionally cast baseline.
The treatment will cause only a negligible reduction in magnetocaloric effect relative to the conventionally cast baseline.
An overly long anneal may cause undesirable grain growth or phase transformations.
Lower rapid-solidification cooling rates may cause undesirable grain growth or phase transformations and reduce the magnetocaloric response.
